newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UAE offset scheme says it will not ease demands.
newsitem.headline: UAE offset scheme says it will not ease demands.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates offset programme, which has been criticised by Western arms makers as too demanding, said on Tuesday it would not consider dropping any of its requirements tied to military sales.
The UAE requires companies it buys weapons from to invest part of the value of the contract in joint ventures with local investors.
"Of course not. We will not change any of the conditions," Mohammad al-Mazroui, UAE Offsets Group (UOG) deputy chairman, told Reuters.
"We think that we can achieve our goals easily. We don't see any difficulties."
An offset official said arms makers had urged the UOG to drop some of its demands.
Some arms manufacturers complain of limited investment opportunities in the Gulf Arab state blessed with immense petrodollars that has emerged as a prized player in the international arms bazaar.
The UAE has lured major Western firms which have set up offices here to lobby for their high-tech weaponry and work out offset proposals -- a task that industry sources say can take years.

One major complaint is that defence companies are required to invest in projects with local investors in 49/51 percent joint ventures that generate added value to the UAE over a period of seven years equivalent to 60 percent of the value of the sales contract.
Firms that fail to do so are obliged to pay the equivalent of 8.5 percent of that 60 percent and are barred from doing business in the UAE.
"In Europe, sometimes you face a requirement of over 100 percent, but in Europe, there are places to invest," said a Western defence source.
"Where are you going to put your money here?" he added.

Mazroui said the problem was not a lack of investment opportunities but the fact that arms makers had to adjust to investing in non-military ventures -- everything from clothing to mobile solar energy generators.
"It's difficult. This is not their environment. They have to find the know-how," he said.
The UOG was launched in July 1990 when the UAE activated a plan to buy high-tech weapons worth billions of dollars.
So far, Western arms companies and their local partners have invested 950 million dirhams ($259 million) in offset schemes, Mazroui said.
Eighteen projects ranging from a shipbuilding company to a medical diagnostic centre have been launched.
Offset officials declined to give profit figures for the projects, citing confidentiality agreements.
